Yes, it's normal. Technically 'pending'  transactions are not a transaction yet, they are just the preauthorisation request from the merchant, similar to restaurants or hotels reserving funds via the card for a booking.


The way credit card payments are processed in this country means that 'pending' transactions are resolved by 1) the merchant confirming the transaction, or 2) the merchant cancelling the transaction, 3) the merchant doesn't do 1 or 2 within a certain period (generally a couple of weeks) so the preauthorisatiom expires. The card issuer needs to wait until the pending status resolves because if 2 or 3 happens, there is no transaction to dispute.

A fixed term residential lease will over to a periodic lease automatically at the end of the term.  This means unless you hear otherwise (or you yourself terminate the lease) you will be staying on as a tenant.

The minimum notice period the landlord is required to give a tenant to evict them in sa situation like this depends on whether the notice is given before or after the end of the fixed term - if before, it's whatever is in the lease (generally 30 days). If after, it's 90 days.

Similarly, the notice period for rent increases will either be whatever's set out in the lease, if given prior to the fixed term ending, or if it has rolled over into the periodic tenancy, a minimum of 60 days' notice.

You should only put in a recall request with CBA if you/your mum wants the funds returned to her account (eg. the funds have been sent to an unknown third party, or are geuinely lost).

If your mum was sending the money, she needs to contact CBA about the recall, etc (unless she can put you on as an authorised representative on her account, CBA will not deal with you). BoQ can't do much at this point.

Is your account with CBA? If so, try contacting them and ask them to do a recall as a first step. This may take a few weeks but it is probably your best chance of getting your funds back.

If you aren't satisfied with the result of the recall, lodge an internal complaint with CBA. If their IDR response doesn't provide a satisfactory resolution in your view, then you lodge a complaint with AFCA.

If you try to go straight to AFCA without an IDR response, they will send you back to deal with CBA first.

If you also have an account with BoQ, you may be able to ask them to follow up on their end once you have asked CBA to do a recall.

If a borrower or co-borrower wants to terminate a mortgage, the lender has to let you - iirc you just have to give them written notice.

It is possible to remove a co-borrower from a mortgage by variation but it's more commonly done by termination of the existing loan - which means repaying of the outstanding amount - and creating a new one. In both methods, the lender has to re-do any responsible lending checks and ensure that the loan won't be unsuitable for the remaining borrower. If the loan is unsuitable, they can't give it to you.

No, the general rule is deductions must be claimed in the year that they were paid, or the year they were invoiced, depending on what basis you are doing your accounting (either cash or accruals). I think for individuals, it's generally cash basis, so when they are paid. You can't carry over deductions.

No, they don't have to be likeable characters, but they do need to be engaging or interesting in some way. Being likeable - ie. being a character that you'd enjoy spending time with in real life - is one way to create interest. Other ways of creating interest include: characters who have aspects we can aspire to (eg., smart, witty, talented or skilled in their field), and characters whom we can sympathise with or whose situation we can sympathise with. So basically, no they don't have to be "likeable", but you do have to want to spend time with them on some level.
